title: Improving branch-and-cut performance by random sampling
contribution: A root-sampling scheme that runs the default root cut loop and heuristics from K-1 different optimal LP bases, pools all cuts and solutions into one final run, reduces root variability and became the CPLEX 12.5.1 default with K = 2 (pp. 4, 7, 12, 17).
problem_entry: Entered from a measured anomaly (Danna's 10teams example, 0 vs 1,426 nodes, p. 2); dual degeneracy of the first LP taken as the first source of variability (pp. 2-3), shown solver-independent on CPLEX, GUROBI, XPRESS by 10 permutations (p. 5, Fig. 1 p. 6).
key_idea: Sample the optimal face: K-1 root runs from different optimal bases (via CPX_PARAM_RANDOMSEED), pool cuts and solutions, one final run from the enriched root; only the starting basis changes; K steers stability vs speed (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: General MIP, structure of A not exploited (p. 1); dual-degenerate root LPs presumed (pp. 2, 5); MIPLIB 2010 benchmark+primal (121; exclusions pp. 9-11) and 3,221-model CPLEX testbed (p. 12); preprocess once so all runs share one space (p. 8).
experiments: Deterministic ticks, 10^7 limit, shifted geometric means (p. 8); root K = 10 over 10 seeds cuts integrality gap 56.91% to 35.81% (Table 1, p. 10); tree ~15% fewer ticks, 25% fewer nodes over 5 seeds (Table 2, p. 11); product test on 3,221 models with classes defined via both solvers, 5 seeds, ratios 0.97-0.99 (pp. 13-16); losses printed but not discussed, no statistical test (pp. 11, 16-17).
positioning: Credits Danna 2008, MIPLIB 2010, Lodi-Tramontani (p. 2); places the scheme beside SAT restarts, bet-and-run, Achterberg's cut filtering, CutsComm, ParaSCIP racing; novelty narrowed to basis selection, no critique (p. 3).
writing: Labelled "Our contribution." paragraph turning variability into opportunity (p. 3); K's two uses as a list (p. 4); CPLEX default announced and repeated (pp. 4, 17); parenthetical hedges and scare quotes (pp. 7, 11); tables carry the argument.
limits_future: Tree variability untouched and named the main open question (pp. 11, 17); large K may not pay in time (p. 4); K > 2 not worth it in CPLEX (p. 12); preprocessing once only approximates default CPLEX (p. 9); adoption stated by authors, no release note cited (p. 1).

method_links.note: spread measured before it is used (10 permutations on 3 solvers; 10 seeds at root), seeds in every table, then exploited; seed-only baseline cpxdef is the control; public seed parameter rather than internal basis loading
step 4: all short runs merged into one root instead of betting on one run as bet-and-run does; where it does not pay is printed (tree stability, K > 2)
classes defined by both solvers; baseline same code with K = 1 and identical settings; exclusions with reasons; sampling-time accounting argued both ways; time-limit bias named
solver's own cut loop and heuristics do the work, only the starting basis changes; seed parameter replaces random pivots
separators and heuristics left alone, the root basis the loop starts from is changed; motive is variance, not a stalling loop

transferable: (D2) Give the scheme one parameter that moves it between two goals: a large sample count to study and reduce variability, a small one for the shipped default (pp. 4, 7, 12).
(D4) Preprocess once and give every sample and the final run that same model, so that cuts and incumbents from different runs live in one space (p. 8).

(D5) Simulate a parallel scheme sequentially without flattering it: restart the final run from scratch, inject the pooled information only where a parallel version would have it (end of root, through callbacks), and charge time with a rule that neither credits zero ticks nor drops the instances solved during sampling (pp. 9-11).

(D5) Before proposing a variance remedy, show the variance is solver-independent: 10 row and column permutations per instance on three solvers, the per-instance variability score (standard deviation over mean), pairwise scatter plots (p. 5, Fig. 1 p. 6).
(D5) Root-node stability table: integrality, primal and dual gaps against known optima, with the mean and the mean per-instance standard deviation over 10 seeds (pp. 9-10).

(D5) Vendor-style class reporting: [n,10k] (solved by at least one arm, at least n seconds for one) and [n,10k) (solved by both), the "affected" subset with differing node and iteration counts, time-limit hits per side, all repeated for 5 seeds (pp. 13-14).
(D5) On a shared cluster report deterministic ticks and state the shifts of the geometric means (10^3 ticks, 10 nodes) (p. 8).
coauthors: Andrea Lodi, Michele Monaci, Domenico Salvagnin, Andrea Tramontani

title: Redesigning Benders decomposition for large-scale facility location
contribution: A redesigned Benders scheme on stock CPLEX (allocation variables projected out, fat/slim masters, in-out root stabilization, closed-form and exact-QP separators) that solves 7 open UFLLIB instances, improves 22 best-known values and solves qUFL instances with up to 40 million variables (pp. 2-3, 19).
problem_entry: Entered from scale: location models with millions of allocation variables where MILP solvers struggle and Lagrangian methods dominate (pp. 1-2); working hypothesis that dropped exact decompositions need a redesign, "sleeping beauties" (pp. 1-2); Benders for UFL left 30+ years (p. 6); qUFL as MINLP test problem (pp. 2, 4).
key_idea: Replace x_ij by w_j (fat) or w_sum (slim) bounded by generalized Benders cuts separated at every node of stock CPLEX branch-and-cut, with in-out stabilization of the root loop; Kelley kept in the tree (pp. 5, 10-14, 19).
assumptions: UFL with linear c_ij >= 0, full allocatability (p. 3); qUFL with unit demands, perspective baseline (p. 4); at least 2 open facilities, small cases enumerated (p. 5); GB cuts need convexity and CQs, y* > 0 handled in §4.1 (pp. 5, 7, 11-12); UFLLIB, Körkel-Ghosh, ORLIB, random qUFL up to 2000 x 10000 (pp. 16-18); uncapacitated only (p. 19).
proof_devices: GB cut from a subgradient of Lagrangian multipliers under KKT, after Geoffrion (eq. 18, p. 5)
continuous knapsack solved by Dantzig's critical-item rule, certified by equal primal and dual cost (p. 6); closed-form cut, only n distinct cuts per customer (p. 7)
ad hoc QP routine (Algorithm 1, p. 9) proved by a monotonicity lemma on beta (Lemma 3.1) and a KKT check (Theorem 3.1) (p. 10)
projection argument: fat and slim masters give the same bound (p. 11)
2 epsilon trick: separate at y* + 2 epsilon, cuts always valid (p. 12)
experiments: Xeon E3-1220V2, 16 GB, 4 threads, untuned settings (p. 16); one-instance traces on gs250a-1: Kelley stuck vs in-out root in 0.19 s / 0.04 s (pp. 13-14, Fig. 1); fat vs slim on MT1 (Fig. 2, p. 15); seven open UFL instances solved (Table 1, p. 17); 22 KG best-knowns improved (p. 18, Table 2 p. 23); qUFL up to four orders faster than the perspective model with MIQCPSTRAT = 1 (Tables 3-5, pp. 18-19, 24-25); no seeds or repetitions for exact runs, no profiles.
positioning: Against the Lagrangian state of the art (Posta et al., Beltran-Royo et al.) via solved instances and best-knowns (pp. 3, 17); in-out credited to Applegate et al., Ben-Ameur and Neto, Fischetti-Salvagnin, Naoum-Sawaya-Elhedhli; bundle methods named stronger (p. 12); QP routines and Margot credited (pp. 8, 16); critique of the habit of judging cuts by polyhedral strength (p. 12).
writing: Working hypothesis in the abstract (p. 1); scare-quoted coinages (pp. 1-2, 8); surprise marked twice (pp. 3, 18); key ingredient flagged at the head of §4.2 (p. 12); colloquial asides (Pavlov's aversion, p. 11); ellipsoid analogy (p. 12); impact as two bullets (p. 19).
limits_future: Practical big-data instances still not solvable directly (p. 2); 50 linear KG instances open (p. 17); Kelley kept in tree (p. 14); no real bundle method (p. 12); capacitated case not immediate (p. 19); future: connected FL, ring-star, median cycle, traveling purchaser, convex MINLP, nonlinear stochastic programming (p. 19).

method_links.note: allocation variables projected out, then w_j aggregated into w_sum; fat and slim run on the same instances and chosen per cost class by measurement

convergence put down to the point to cut, not cut strength; in-out with stabilizer at all ones moved halfway; all loops call the same separator; 2 epsilon alone rescues Kelley; stabilization at root only, with reason

stock MILP solver plus one plugged-in separator solved open instances 2500-10 and 3000-100 in under 15 minutes on a PC; simple in-out instead of bundle; no qUFL-specific heuristics; own sub-MIP heuristics through the solver
(partial) compact baseline run with its best CPLEX setting (MIQCPSTRAT = 1) while the new code runs untuned; Lagrangian comparisons go through solved status and best-knowns, not a common harness
seeds only as a resource (four concurrent seeded runs, best kept); no seeds for exact runs; with orders-of-magnitude speed-ups this does not threaten conclusions

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: closed-form subproblem oracle with a proof
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: critical-item closed-form cut for linear costs and proved exact QP routine (Algorithm 1, Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.1)
perspective skipped near 0/1, 2 epsilon trick, 10^-9 tolerances, Margot-style validity test; also S016 pp. 19-21

transferable: (D4) In-out root loop with its constants: y~ := (1,...,1); each iteration y~ := (y~ + y*)/2 and separate at lambda y* + (1 - lambda) y~ + delta (1,...,1) with lambda = 0.2, delta = 2 epsilon; after 5 iterations without bound improvement set lambda = 1, after 5 more delta = 0, after 5 more stop and drop slack cuts; drop slack cuts every 5th iteration (pp. 12-13).
(D4) When the Benders subproblem is a continuous knapsack, sort the costs, find the critical item and write the cut in closed form; only n distinct cuts exist per customer (pp. 6-7).

(D4) Inside a separator, replace a general QP solver by a small exact routine with a proof (truncate the violated bounds and re-solve on the residual set; Algorithm 1, Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.1; pp. 8-10).

(D4) Near degenerate values, skip a numerically risky strengthening (perspective off for y*_i < 10^-5 or > 1 - 10^-5) and separate at y* + 2 epsilon, which keeps cuts valid and also helps plain Kelley (p. 12).

(D4) For integer master points add one aggregated optimality cut in the lazy callback instead of flooding the pool with per-customer cuts (p. 15); add tree cuts as local so the solver can purge them, and cap rounds per node (20; 2,000 at the root) (p. 14).
(D4) Cut-validity stress test: fix the incumbent, perturb 80% of its entries by 10^-9 to 10^-1, separate, add, re-solve, 10,000 times, and dump the model on failure (p. 16).

(D5) One-instance trace figure: the same separator under three point-selection policies, log time axis, active cuts at the end of the root and of the run (Fig. 1, p. 13); then fat against slim on a second instance (Fig. 2, p. 15).
(D5) Run the compact baseline with the solver option that suits it best, and say so (MIQCPSTRAT = 1, p. 18).

title: A new general-purpose algorithm for mixed-integer bilevel linear programs
contribution: Extends the authors' 2016 intersection-cut branch-and-cut for MIBLPs with FUB cuts, follower preprocessing, new IC families chosen by separation MILPs and a numerically safe IC derivation, tested on 874 instances and released with solver and optimal values (pp. 3, 7, 11-22, 37).
problem_entry: Entered from hierarchical applications and the scarcity of generic MIBLP solvers despite NP/Σ2-hardness (pp. 4-5); direct entry is the authors' own 2016 solver on a MILP solver (p. 6); obstacle: arbitrarily weak HPR bounds need deep cuts early (p. 10).
key_idea: Keep 2016 branch-and-cut on the HPR and add locally valid FUB cuts (Thm 1), follower fixing (Thm 2), new IC families from bilevel-free sets (Thms 3-6), separation MILPs choosing the set (pp. 17-18), numerically safe IC derivation (Alg. 1, pp. 19-20); default MIX++ (pp. 29, 31-32).
assumptions: Optimistic MIBLP with integer and continuous variables at both levels (pp. 3, 5); Assumption 1 J_F ⊆ J_x for finite convergence, 2 bounded HPR, 3 integer slacks for some ICs (p. 8); d integer (p. 17); all tested leaders integer (pp. 8, 22); 874 instances in ten classes incl. MIPLIB-derived, interdiction solved as general (pp. 22-23, Table 1 p. 25); wrong-coefficient repository warned (pp. 22-23).
proof_devices: restriction of the follower overestimates the value function (Theorem 1, p. 11)
dominance argument for fixing with strict signs in the optimistic setting (Theorem 2, pp. 11-12)
integer slacks turn interior into the closed set (Theorem 4, p. 14)
half-space test with variable bounds removes facets (Theorem 5, Corollary 1, p. 15)
integrality of linking leader variables gives the hypercube (Theorem 6, p. 16)
IC derivation through the disjunctive interpretation (Glover; Glover and Klingman), validity on original data so error only reduces violation (pp. 18-20)
experiments: Xeon E5-2670v2, 12 GB, 4 threads, 3,600 s (p. 22); ablations vs SEP1/SEP2 with cumulative speed-up charts (Fig. 2, pp. 26-27) and MIPLIB final-gap charts (pp. 27-28, Fig. 3); Dolan-Moré profiles on commonly solved, mostly easy instances (p. 29); hypercube ICs (Table 2, p. 33); literature comparisons against rivals' published times with an unexplained 2-5x hardware factor (pp. 33-38, Tables 3-6); no seeds, repetitions or significance tests under nondeterministic parallel mode (p. 20); losses in tables not named in text (pp. 35-38).
positioning: Reviews generic MIBLP methods (Moore-Bard, MibS, Xu-Wang, Xu, Caramia-Mari, parametric IP, Tang et al.) and names own 2016 solver the state of the art (pp. 8-10); credits Balas, Xu, Glover/Glover-Klingman (pp. 7, 12-13, 18-19); distinguishes from Audet et al. (p. 10); contrasts DeNegre (p. 21); leaves out nonlinear bilevel methods as a biased comparison (p. 33).
writing: Contribution bullet list (p. 7); superlatives for scope and outcome (pp. 3, 22, 37); implementation section justified by reproducibility (p. 20); each ingredient with a short theorem and proof (pp. 11-16); rare hedges ("hopefully" deep ICs, p. 13).
limits_future: Continuous leader variables in follower excluded and untested (pp. 8, 22); only hypercube ICs without integer slacks (pp. 16, 34); IC effectiveness decays, round limit (p. 21); CPLEX heuristics off (p. 21); future: interdiction specialization, nonlinear settings (p. 37); 300+ unsolved headline includes never-tested classes, 238 on earlier classes (p. 25).

method_links.note: bilevel solver on top of a MILP solver handling cuts, heuristics, propagation, numerics, threads; each critical sub-decision is itself a MILP solved with the same solver; CPLEX cuts stay on

transferable: (D4) For any value-function constraint d^T y <= Φ(x), derive a locally valid cut at each node by restricting the inner problem to its worst case over the node's bounds and solving that MILP once per node (Theorem 1, p. 11; once per node, p. 21).

(D4) Fix inner variables whose optimal value is forced whatever the outer decision (positive cost and non-negative column: lower bound; the mirror case: upper bound), with strict signs in the optimistic case (Theorem 2, pp. 11-12).
(D4) Choose the convex set behind an intersection cut by an auxiliary MILP that maximizes the number of removable facets (pp. 17-18).

(D4) Derive intersection cuts in a numerically safe way: compute coefficients from the original rows rather than tableau entries, so precision errors cost violation only; clip integer-variable coefficients at 1; drop cuts with dynamism above 10^6 or relative violation below 10^-6 (|rhs| + 1) (pp. 19-21).
(D4) In the lazy-constraint callback, turn every rejected candidate into a repaired solution (solve the inner problem at x*, check the outer constraints) and offer it as an incumbent (p. 21).
(D4) Branch first on outer variables that link to the inner problem (priorities 2, 1, 0; p. 21).
(D5) Ablate each new ingredient by toggles on the previous best code (+F, +P, ++), with cumulative speed-up charts using a 1 s shift and final-gap charts for the unsolved instances (pp. 26-28).
(D5) State which instances a performance profile contains, and that most of them are easy (p. 29).
(D8) Release the solver, the instances and their optimal values with the paper (pp. 3, 7, 22, 42).
coauthors: Ivana Ljubić, Michele Monaci, Markus Sinnl
